Assignment 04 / Sculpting for Design

Wire Sculpture

Drawing in space: a dinosaur’s volume and a dancer’s gesture, built from bent and wrapped wire.

Wire · Volume · Gesture

The course exercise explored wire as a sculptural material through animal and human forms. Medha chose a brachiosaurus and a dancer, working between a substantial body and a more open, gestural figure.

01

Thinking through a line

The brainstorming drawings test several possible structures. Some studies explore repeated loops and enclosed volumes; others consider a figure in motion and an animal with a long neck.

These sketches provide a bridge between drawing and construction. A line on paper can simply describe an outline, but a wire line also needs to hold its shape in space. The studies make it possible to consider the body, limbs, and overall pose before bending the material.

02

Building a brachiosaurus

Medha wanted to make a brachiosaurus, choosing a herbivorous dinosaur as her animal subject. The finished piece uses many overlapping lengths of wire to establish the torso, with a long neck, projecting head, and four legs giving it a recognisable silhouette.

The photographs reveal how wrapped wire creates both surface and volume. Gaps remain between the strands, so the body can be read as a solid mass while still allowing a view through its construction.

03

A familiar movement

For the human form, Medha returned to Mohiniyattam, the Kerala dance form she has trained in for over ten years. She wanted to make a dancer’s figure, connecting the material exercise with a practice she knows through movement.

The raised arm and bent limbs make the pose readable with relatively little material. Unlike the densely wrapped dinosaur, the dancer relies on an open outline and the relationship between the different parts of the body.

04

Two ways to occupy space

Seen together, the sculptures explore different possibilities within the same material. The dinosaur accumulates wire into a rounded body, while the dancer uses a more economical structure to describe a pose.

The project connects the physical behaviour of wire with two kinds of observation: recognising an animal’s proportions and recalling the gesture of a trained dancer.
